results.summary: This analog bandgap reference is designed to provide a constant 1.2V output from a 3.3V supply. It is tested by placing the chip in an oven and measuring the output voltage across different temperatures. No external hardware is required for basic operation, though a multimeter is needed to measure the output. The documentation is minimal, providing only the basic function and test method, with no details on the circuit topology or performance.

This design implements a minimal perceptron-based branch predictor for RISC-V processors, using SPI to receive branch addresses and ground truth directions. It is tested with CocoTB and a functional simulation that parses Spike execution logs, and it requires external hardware to drive and read its pins. Notable features include latch-based memory from a third-party repository and detailed documentation with waveforms. The design is not single-cycle due to memory constraints and includes debug outputs for monitoring internal state.

This current-mode bandgap reference provides a stable 1V voltage and 5.6uA current, with an integrated testbuffer for measurement. It is tested by applying external bias and control signals, and requires a multimeter, power supply, and optionally an oven for temperature stability tests. Silicon results show the voltage output at 1.15V and current at 6.9uA, with minor documentation errors noted. The design includes an 8-bit trim for process variations and can be enabled or disabled via a control pin.

This design implements a Dempsey-Gorman 8-bit segmented DAC using two resistor ladders without voltage buffering. It is tested by setting the 8-bit input and measuring the analog output voltage, which should map to the 0V to 3.3V range. External hardware such as a multimeter or oscilloscope is required to measure the output. The documentation is brief but sufficient, referencing an external tutorial for architecture details.

The VSLC is a small PLC-like stack machine controller with 8 inputs, 8 outputs, timers, and servo control, inspired by relay logic and early PLCs. It is programmed via an external EEPROM over SPI and executes scan cycles to handle control tasks such as model train crossing gates. External hardware includes an EEPROM emulator or actual EEPROM, and the design includes a compiler and disassembler for program development. Notable features include edge detection between scan cycles and complementary timer outputs.

This is a simple alarm clock that compares internal hour and minute counters against user-set alarm values and asserts an alarm output when they match. It is tested with a provided testbench that sets alarm values and observes the alarm and time outputs. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself, though the design uses inout pins for some signals due to pin limitations. The project was sponsored by MITRE and MIT/LL Beaver Works Summer Institute, indicating an educational origin.

This is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA SoC capable of booting Linux, featuring external SPI flash and PSRAM, a UART, and a SPI peripheral. It is tested by building a system image and loading it into the SPI flash, then running at 30 MHz (max tested 34.5 MHz). External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod for flash and PSRAM, and a UART connection for communication. Notable for being a full Linux-capable SoC on a Tiny Tapeout chip.

This design allows an analog supply to power a digital counter, with the warning that the analog supply resistor must be removed before enabling to avoid destroying the digital logic. It is tested by connecting a variable power supply to the analog supply and observing the counter outputs. External hardware includes a variable PSU. The documentation is minimal and emphasizes the destructive risk if misused.

This is an analog level shifter experiment that operates down to around 0.2V, designed by Sylvain Munaut. It is tested by applying an input signal and observing the output, requiring an adjustable power supply, a soldering iron to remove a resistor, and an oscilloscope. The design improves upon traditional level shifters that only work down to about 1V. The documentation includes a schematic and a graph showing a 0.2V input resulting in a full 1.8V swing output.

This design is a stylish ring oscillator built from 21 SkullFET inverters, generating a square wave with a simulated frequency of about 169.2 MHz. It is tested by connecting an oscilloscope to the divided outputs, as the full-speed outputs are too fast for GPIO pins. No external hardware is required beyond an oscilloscope. Notable for its use of SkullFET transistors and the inclusion of frequency dividers for observability.
